lines.text: More than six hundred islands scattered across the Pacific, with stone money, a city built on a reef and a long line of foreign rulers. This is Micronesia.
On the island of Yap, people quarried great stone discs and used them as money, some of them taller than a person.
Off Pohnpei, the Saudeleur rulers built Nan Madol, a city of stone platforms and canals laid out on the coral reef.
On Kosrae, the island's rulers built their own stone town at Lelu, with high walls of basalt.
From the sixteenth century Spain claimed these islands, the Carolines, as part of its Pacific lands, until the end of the eighteen nineties.
Tosiwo Nakayama, born in 1931, would become the first president of an independent Micronesia.
After Germany and then Japan held the islands, war came. In 1944 American planes struck the Japanese fleet base at Chuuk.
After the war the islands became a United Nations trust territory, run by the United States.
Wesley Simina, born in 1961, would become president in 2023.
A Compact of Free Association was agreed with the United States, giving the islands self-rule with American support.
In 1986 the Federated States of Micronesia began, four island states in free association with the United States.
In 1989 Palikir, on Pohnpei, became the capital of the young nation.
From stone money to self-rule, Micronesia keeps its own course across the open Pacific.
